title: Cell Identity, Cell State and Disease

generated.pipeline: extract -> Codex draft -> Codex accuracy gate and fix

cards.front: A tissue can change because {{c1::which cells are there}} changes, not only because its cells behave differently.
cards.back: A change in cell composition can change the tissue without a change within any cell type.
cards.quote: A tissue can change because which cells are there changes, not only because its cells behave differently.

cards.front: In the simple branching model, the expected progenitor multiplier per division is {{c1::m = 2p(PP) + p(PD)}}.
cards.back: PP contributes two progenitors, PD one and DD none.
cards.quote: each round of division multiplies a clone's expected progenitors by m = 2 × p(PP) + p(PD).

cards.front: In the simple branching model, how do daughter fate and division rate affect progenitor-clone growth differently?
cards.back: Daughter fate sets m and therefore growth per round; division rate sets how often that multiplication occurs.
cards.quote: Daughter fate sets m, so it decides whether the clone grows; division rate sets only how often the multiplying happens.

cards.front: How many progenitors remain after PP, PD and DD divisions, respectively?
cards.back: Two, one and zero progenitors, respectively.
cards.quote: A PP division leaves two progenitors, a PD division one and a DD division none

cards.front: A progenitor has PP, PD and DD probabilities of 0.25, 0.50 and 0.25. What is m, and what happens to the expected pool per round?
cards.back: m = 2(0.25) + 0.50 = 1.0. Each round leaves the expected progenitor pool unchanged.
cards.quote: Balanced outcomes of 0.25, 0.50 and 0.25 (PP, PD, DD) give m = 0.50 + 0.50 = 1.0.

cards.front: A mutant has PP, PD and DD probabilities of 0.35, 0.50 and 0.15. Starting with 100 progenitors, how many are expected after three rounds with no death?
cards.quote: Start with 100 mutant progenitors and no death: after three rounds there are about 100 × 1.2 × 1.2 × 1.2 ≈ 173

cards.front: A progenitor population has m = 1 but divides twice as often as its neighbours. Over the same time, what happens to its expected progenitor pool, and why?
cards.back: It stays unchanged on average. Every round multiplies the pool by 1, so performing more rounds still leaves the expectation at its starting value.
cards.quote: With m = 1, dividing twice as often leaves the expected pool unchanged.

cards.front: A population starts with 100 progenitors and has m = 1.2. How many are expected after six rounds rather than three?
cards.back: After six rounds: 100(1.2)^6 = 298.6, about 300. After three: 100(1.2)^3 = 172.8, about 173.
cards.quote: at m = 1.2, six rounds instead of three give about 300 expected progenitors instead of about 173.

cards.front: Why can clones with the same fixed daughter-fate probabilities reach very different sizes?
cards.back: The rule is an average over clones. Early DD outcomes can eliminate one clone, whereas early PP outcomes can make another large.
cards.quote: A single clone is a run of chance: one whose first divisions are DD vanishes; one that rolls PP early grows large.

cards.front: Only surviving wild-type clones are measured late, and they are larger than at labelling. Does that show wild-type m exceeds 1? Explain.
cards.back: No. Even with m = 1, chance eliminates some clones while early PP outcomes enlarge survivors. The rule is that m describes the average over all clones.
cards.quote: So surviving wild-type clones grow too, and mutant clone growth shows an advantage only against wild-type clones labelled the same way.

cards.front: EdU is incorporated into DNA only during {{c1::S phase}}, while a cell copies its DNA.
cards.back: A short EdU pulse marks cells synthesizing DNA at that moment.
cards.quote: EdU, a mimic of the DNA building block thymidine, is built into DNA only during S phase
cards.section: Rate or fate? The mouse experiment

cards.front: What different questions do an EdU pulse and an EdU pulse-chase answer in basal epithelium?
cards.back: The pulse estimates which cells are copying DNA; the chase reveals whether labelled daughters remain basal or move up.
cards.quote: A pulse-chase labels them, then waits to see where their daughters end up: still basal, or moved up.
cards.section: Rate or fate? The mouse experiment

cards.front: Design an experiment to distinguish faster division from altered daughter fate in expanding Notch1-mutant mouse oesophageal clones.
cards.back: Compare sparse mutant and wild-type labelled clones. Use a one-hour EdU pulse for division and a pulse-chase for fate, while following clone sizes over time.
cards.why: Faster division predicts more pulse labelling; a fate tilt predicts similar pulse labelling but more labelled mutant daughters remaining basal after the chase.
cards.quote: Estimate division rate with a one-hour EdU pulse, and fate with a pulse-chase. Follow clone sizes over time.
cards.section: Rate or fate? The mouse experiment

cards.front: Mutant clones expand but have the same one-hour EdU-labelled basal fraction as wild-type clones. If daughter fate is tilted, what should an EdU chase show?
cards.back: More labelled mutant daughters should remain basal. Equal pulse labelling argues against faster division, while basal retention supports reduced differentiation.
cards.quote: A fate tilt predicts similar labelling after the pulse but, after the chase, more labelled mutant daughters still basal.
cards.section: Rate or fate? The mouse experiment

cards.front: Why is the fraction of cells labelled by a short EdU pulse only a proxy for division rate?
cards.back: It also depends on S-phase duration and on how many basal cells remain cycling progenitors.
cards.quote: the fraction in S phase also depends on how long S phase lasts and on how many basal cells are still cycling progenitors.
cards.section: Rate or fate? The mouse experiment

cards.front: In the mouse experiment, what does inducible Cre lineage tracing allow researchers to follow?
cards.back: It marks a few cells and all descendants, can delete floxed Notch1, and activates a visible YFP reporter.
cards.quote: Inducible Cre lineage tracing marks a few cells and all their descendants.
cards.section: Rate or fate? The mouse experiment

cards.front: What explained the expansion of mouse oesophageal clones lacking one or both Notch1 copies?
cards.back: They expanded without a higher division rate; tracking supported more progenitor and fewer differentiating daughters per division.
cards.quote: mouse clones lacking one or both copies of Notch1 expanded without a higher division rate
cards.section: Rate or fate? The mouse experiment

cards.front: Why must a neighbour leave when an extra progenitor is retained in a full basal epithelial layer?
cards.back: Space is balanced alongside daughter fate: the basal layer has no spare room, so an added cell requires another cell to leave.
cards.quote: a basal layer has no spare room, so an extra cell needs a neighbour to leave.

cards.front: Crowding increases epithelial-cell extrusion, and most extruding cells lack active caspase-3. What conclusion does this support?
cards.back: Crowding can extrude cells before apoptosis. Increased extrusion links the event to crowding, while absent active caspase-3 argues the cells were not yet apoptotic.
cards.quote: Crowding pushed out living cells, which then died, probably because they lost the survival signals that attachment to the sheet provides.

cards.front: If normal-looking clones surrounding early oesophageal lesions become more competitive for space, what should happen to lesion persistence?
cards.back: Fewer lesions should persist because stronger surrounding clones remove early lesions more often through competition for space.
cards.quote: Competition for space can protect the tissue.

cards.front: In zebrafish epidermis, Piezo1 knockdown blocks crowding-induced extrusion and produces epidermal cell masses. What role does this support for Piezo1?
cards.back: Piezo1 is needed for this crowding-responsive extrusion in zebrafish: blocking it prevents the exit that normally relieves excess cell density.
cards.quote: Knocking down Piezo1, a channel opened by membrane stretch, blocked this extrusion in zebrafish and produced masses of epidermal cells.

cards.front: Why does filling normal oesophageal lining with Notch1-mutant cells not by itself mean that a tumour has formed?
cards.back: Losing Notch1 can confer a space-winning fate tilt in normal lining yet reduce tumour growth in the mouse tumour model.
cards.quote: Winning space in normal lining is not the same as growing as a tumour.

cards.front: For amounts expressed per cell, what does a bulk tissue measurement average?
cards.back: It is a weighted average of each cell type's per-cell level, weighted by the type's abundance.
cards.quote: an average over every cell, weighted by how many of each kind there are.

cards.front: Type T expresses X at 50 units per cell and other cells at 5. T rises from 20% to 40%, with no per-cell change. What bulk fold change results?
cards.quote: A bulk experiment would report gene X up 1.6-fold, although no cell regulated it.

cards.front: Bulk RNA for a gene rises, but expression within every single-cell cluster is unchanged. What population-level change could explain the bulk result?
cards.back: The proportions of clusters changed. More cells from a high-expressing type can raise the bulk average without regulation within any type.
cards.quote: Single-cell data would show the same expression inside each cluster and a changed proportion of clusters.

cards.front: Keratinocytes and macrophages differ largely in {{c1::which genes they transcribe}}, not in their genomes.
cards.back: Transcription factors and chromatin help maintain these expression patterns.
cards.quote: What makes a keratinocyte differ from a macrophage is which genes it transcribes

cards.front: How does single-cell RNA sequencing turn dissociated cells into gene-by-cell counts?
cards.back: Each cell's RNA is copied into DNA with a shared cell barcode; pooled DNA is sequenced, sorted by barcode and counted.
cards.quote: Each cell's RNA is captured and copied into DNA tagged with a cell barcode, a short sequence shared by every molecule from that cell.

cards.front: In a single-cell RNA-seq count matrix, each entry is the {{c1::number of molecules or reads for one gene in one cell}}.
cards.back: Rows are genes and columns are cells.
cards.quote: one row per gene, one column per cell, each entry the number of molecules (or reads) counted.

cards.front: How can tissue dissociation create a false difference in cluster proportions between conditions?
cards.back: If fragile cell types survive the enzymes differently between samples, their measured proportions change before counting.
cards.quote: if dissociation loses fragile cells preferentially, cluster proportions are biased before you count

cards.front: A stable identity is a cell {{c1::type}}, whereas cycling, stress or activation are cell states within an identity.
cards.back: The type-state boundary depends on the question and the resolution used.
cards.quote: A cell state is variation within that identity: cycling, stressed, activated, early or late in differentiation.

cards.front: Why should a single-cell RNA-seq cluster not automatically be called a cell type?
cards.back: States within one type can form separate clusters, and technical artifacts can also create clusters.
cards.quote: So a cluster is an observation to explain, not a type by definition.

cards.front: A known gene has a zero count in one single-cell RNA-seq cell. What is the most defensible interpretation?
cards.back: No molecule of that RNA was captured and counted in that cell; the zero alone does not establish that the gene was off.
cards.quote: only some RNA molecules are captured

cards.front: A small cluster expresses full T-cell and epithelial keratin programmes. What should be checked before proposing a new hybrid cell type?
cards.back: Check for a doublet: high RNA counts and doublet scores, both programmes in the same barcodes, and a plausible T-cell–epithelial pairing frequency.
cards.quote: The likeliest reading is a doublet, a T cell and an epithelial cell under one barcode

cards.front: A putative cell type appears in several separately processed samples. How would you test whether its cluster reflects biology rather than batch?
cards.back: Check whether cells of that population mix across batches. The rule is that batch effects split cells by processing, whereas a shared biological population can contain cells from several samples.
cards.quote: Batch effects: technical differences between samples processed separately

cards.front: Increasing clustering resolution splits T cells into two clusters, one rich in S-phase and mitosis RNAs. What is the best interpretation?
cards.back: A cycling state within the T-cell type likely formed its own cluster. Higher resolution can separate states rather than reveal new types.
cards.quote: Turned up, a type splits into states or noise; turned down, types merge

cards.front: Markers were found by testing the same expression data used to define clusters. How should the claimed marker support be tested?
cards.back: Confirm it with independent evidence, such as protein. The rule is that selecting and testing on the same differences makes P values too small.
cards.quote: Markers look better supported than they are: P values too small, because the clusters were drawn to differ

cards.front: A stress-associated cluster appears only after enzymatic tissue dissociation. How can you test whether the state existed in the tissue?
cards.back: Compare with fixed tissue or stain in situ. Evidence from intact tissue tests whether dissociation created the stress state in the dish.
cards.quote: Dissociation stress: breaking up tissue perturbs state before capture

cards.front: Pseudotime is a cell's {{c1::distance along an inferred expression path from the chosen start}}.
cards.back: It orders different cells; it does not follow one cell through time.
cards.quote: it arranges cells along a path and gives each a pseudotime, its distance along that inferred path from the start.

cards.front: Why is a pseudotime trajectory neither a movie of one maturing cell nor proof of direction?
cards.back: Sequencing destroys each cell, so different cells are ordered; direction is assumed by choosing which end is the start.
cards.quote: Its direction is an assumption, usually set by choosing which end is the start.

cards.front: A single-cell cluster and pseudotime path suggest a developmental transition driven by factor F. What complementary evidence would test ancestry, causality and annotation?
cards.back: Use lineage tracing for ancestry, perturb F and restore it for causality, and measure defining proteins for annotation. Each test addresses a different inference.
cards.quote: Lineage shows ancestry, perturbation tests cause, and protein checks the annotation.

cards.front: Sister blood progenitors share fate biases that their initial RNA profiles do not reveal. What does this show about expression-based trajectory predictions?
cards.back: They can miss fate information. The rule is that inherited lineage barcodes can reveal related cells and later outcomes that initial RNA profiles did not distinguish.
cards.quote: Sister cells shared fate biases that the RNA profiles had not detected.

cards.front: Why can CITE-seq test a proposed surface-marker annotation more directly than RNA counts alone?
cards.back: RNA does not measure protein; CITE-seq uses DNA-tagged antibodies to measure a surface marker alongside RNA in the same cell.
cards.quote: a surface marker can be measured in the same cell rather than inferred.

cards.front: A {{c1::unique molecular identifier}} lets later copies be collapsed back into one original molecule.
cards.back: It distinguishes original molecules from copies made later.
cards.quote: each molecule also gets a unique molecular identifier, so copies made later can be collapsed back into one original molecule.

cards.front: After quality control and dimension reduction, how are cells converted into clusters in the described workflow?
cards.back: Cells are linked to similar neighbours in a graph; tightly linked groups become clusters.
cards.quote: Cells are linked to their most similar neighbours in a graph, and groups of tightly linked cells become clusters.

cards.front: In the T-versus-other example, T has twice the total RNA per cell. T rises from 20% to 40%; X levels are 50 in T and 5 in others. What RNA-normalized fold change results?
cards.back: Normalize the per-cell gene averages by total RNA. Before: 14/[0.20(2)+0.80(1)] = 11.67. After: 23/[0.40(2)+0.60(1)] = 16.43. Fold = 16.43/11.67 = 1.41.
cards.quote: If bulk data are normalized per unit of RNA, each type also counts in proportion to its RNA content.

cards.front: In a balanced m = 1 model, surviving clones average 6.5 progenitors after 20 rounds, yet the average over all labelled clones remains 1. How can both be true?
cards.back: Most clones disappeared, so the larger survivors are balanced by zeros. The rule is that m = 1 fixes the all-clone expectation, not the size conditional on survival.
cards.quote: about 15 in 100 labelled clones survive 20 rounds and average about 6.5 progenitors
